tracks.name: Scene Foundations
tracks.description: Build the renderer, camera, meshes, lights, and a steady frame loop.

lessons.title: 1. Scene, camera, renderer
lessons.summary: A three.js app always needs a renderer, a scene graph, and a camera.

activities.title: The three core objects
activities.instruction: The renderer draws into a canvas. The scene holds meshes, lights, and groups. The camera decides which part of the scene is visible and how perspective is projected.

activities.title: What the camera controls
activities.question: What does the camera control in a three.js scene?
choices: Which meshes are stored in memory
What part of the scene is visible and how it is projected
How many draw calls the GPU receives
activities.answer: What part of the scene is visible and how it is projected
activities.explanation: The scene stores objects; the camera supplies the view and projection matrices used to render them. A mesh outside the camera frustum is not drawn.

activities.title: Create the three core objects
activities.instruction: Create a `WebGLRenderer`, a `Scene`, and a `PerspectiveCamera`, then render once.

teaching.text: Set up the renderer once, then treat the scene and camera as the inputs to every frame. `antialias: true` smooths edges; capping pixel ratio at 2 keeps high-DPI screens from rendering four times the pixels.
`PerspectiveCamera` takes field of view in degrees, aspect ratio, near plane, and far plane. Keep the near plane as large as your scene allows; tiny near values waste depth precision.

lessons.task: Create the renderer, scene, and perspective camera, then render one frame.
hints: Create the renderer first, then the scene and camera.
Call `renderer.render(scene, camera)` after all three exist.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why cap `devicePixelRatio` instead of rendering at the screen's full physical resolution?

lessons.title: 2. Geometry, material, mesh
lessons.summary: Geometry defines shape, material defines surface, and a Mesh binds them together.

activities.title: One cube, one ground
activities.instruction: `BoxGeometry` stores vertices for a box. `MeshStandardMaterial` describes how light interacts with the surface. `Mesh` combines the two and can be positioned in the scene.

activities.title: Which object binds shape to surface?
activities.question: Which object combines a geometry and a material into something you can add to a scene?
choices: Scene
Mesh
PerspectiveCamera
activities.explanation: A mesh is the drawable pairing of geometry and material. A scene is the container; a camera is the viewpoint.

activities.title: Build a lit cube
activities.instruction: Create a box geometry and a standard material, combine them in a mesh, and add the mesh to the scene.

teaching.text: Think of geometry as vertex data and material as shader settings. Meshes share both freely: one geometry can back a hundred meshes, which saves memory and upload work.
`MeshStandardMaterial` needs light. `MeshBasicMaterial` ignores lights, which is useful for unlit UI helpers but makes a scene look flat.

lessons.task: Build a cube from a box geometry and a standard material, then add it to the scene.
hints: Create the geometry and material separately, then pass both to `new THREE.Mesh(...)`.
Assign the mesh to `cube` and call `scene.add(cube)`.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is sharing one geometry across many meshes usually better than creating a new geometry for each?

lessons.title: 3. Lights and shadows
lessons.summary: Lights make standard materials visible, and shadow maps make depth readable.

activities.title: A key light with a shadow camera
activities.instruction: Enable the renderer's shadow map, set `castShadow` on objects that block light, and `receiveShadow` on surfaces that catch it. A directional light's shadow camera has a limited box, so keep its range tight.

activities.title: Why is the cube black?
activities.question: A cube uses `MeshStandardMaterial` but the scene has no lights. What does the camera show?
choices: The material's base color
A black or nearly black cube
A warning that materials need a camera
activities.answer: A black or nearly black cube
activities.explanation: Standard materials are lit. With no ambient, directional, point, or environment light there is nothing for the surface to reflect.

activities.title: Light the scene and enable shadows
activities.instruction: Enable shadow maps, add a directional light that casts shadows, and make the cube cast one.

teaching.text: A three-point setup is a good default: a key light for shape, a softer fill for detail, and a rim or environment light to separate objects from the background. Start with one key light and add only what the scene needs.
Shadows cost a second render from the light's point of view. Large shadow maps and several shadow-casting lights are common causes of mobile slowdown.

lessons.task: Enable shadows, add a directional key light, and make the cube cast a shadow.
hints: Turn on `renderer.shadowMap.enabled` first.
Set `castShadow = true` on the light and on the cube.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: What makes a shadow map expensive, and how would you reduce that cost on a phone?

lessons.title: 4. Render loop and resize
lessons.summary: Render continuously with an animation loop, and update the camera and renderer whenever the canvas size changes.

activities.title: A loop that survives resizing
activities.instruction: `setAnimationLoop` runs once per animation frame and works with WebXR. A resize handler updates the camera aspect, rebuilds the projection matrix, and resizes the renderer.

activities.title: Why rebuild the projection matrix?
activities.question: After changing `camera.aspect`, why call `camera.updateProjectionMatrix()`?
choices: It reloads the camera's JavaScript file
It bakes the new aspect into the projection matrix used for rendering
It resizes the canvas automatically
activities.answer: It bakes the new aspect into the projection matrix used for rendering
activities.explanation: The projection matrix is derived from the camera's current settings. Changing a property does not rebuild it for you.

activities.title: Keep the canvas in sync
activities.instruction: Start an animation loop, update the camera aspect on resize, and rebuild the projection matrix.

teaching.text: The loop is the heartbeat of the scene: update controls, animate objects, then render. Keep the work inside it small and predictable; allocate objects outside the loop whenever possible.
Observe the canvas container, not always the window. A scene embedded in a resizable panel needs the panel's dimensions.

lessons.task: Add an animation loop and a resize handler that keeps the camera and renderer in sync.
hints: `renderer.setAnimationLoop(() => { ... })` starts the frame loop.
Inside a resize function, set `camera.aspect = width / height`, update the projection matrix, then call `renderer.setSize(width, height)`.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is it risky to create new vectors or geometries inside the animation loop on every frame?

tracks.name: Motion & Interaction
tracks.description: Animate with time, orbit the camera, pick objects, and load real models.

lessons.title: 5. Frame-rate-independent motion
lessons.summary: Multiply movement by elapsed time so the scene behaves the same at 60, 120, or 30 fps.

activities.title: One radian per second
activities.instruction: `Clock.getDelta()` returns seconds since the previous call. Multiplying by delta turns a per-frame guess into a real speed. Clamp large deltas after a tab switch so objects do not jump.

activities.title: Why not add a fixed amount?
activities.question: Why is `cube.rotation.y += 0.01` a problem compared with using delta time?
choices: It rotates in the wrong direction
The speed changes with the display's refresh rate
It disables the renderer's animation loop
activities.answer: The speed changes with the display's refresh rate
activities.explanation: A 120 Hz screen runs the loop twice as often as a 60 Hz screen. Delta time makes the motion depend on seconds, not frame count.

activities.title: Rotate at one radian per second
activities.instruction: Create a clock and rotate the cube by `delta` each frame inside an animation loop.

teaching.text: Delta time is the bridge between game logic and hardware. Movement, decay, and cooldowns should all be expressed per second, then scaled by the actual time that passed.
`Math.min(clock.getDelta(), 0.1)` prevents a huge jump when the browser tab was backgrounded or the machine hiccuped.

lessons.task: Rotate the cube at one radian per second using a clock and delta time.
hints: Create the clock once, outside the loop.
Read `const delta = clock.getDelta()` each frame and add it to `cube.rotation.y`.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: What visual bug appears when a long pause produces a very large delta?

lessons.title: 6. OrbitControls
lessons.summary: Orbit controls turn the camera into a navigable object without writing pointer math yourself.

activities.title: Import, attach, update
activities.instruction: `OrbitControls` attaches to the renderer's canvas and updates the camera's position around a target. With damping on, call `update()` every frame so the motion eases to a stop.

activities.title: Why call update?
activities.question: Why does `enableDamping = true` require `controls.update()` every frame?
choices: The controls need to reload the model
Damping eases the camera toward its target over several frames
It recompiles the material
activities.answer: Damping eases the camera toward its target over several frames
activities.explanation: Without `update()`, the easing never advances. The camera only follows the pointer's final delta.

activities.title: Add orbit controls
activities.instruction: Create `OrbitControls` for the camera and canvas, enable damping, and update them in the loop.

teaching.text: `OrbitControls` is in the addons entry point, not the core `three` module. Browsers need an import map so both `three` and `three/addons/` resolve to the same installed version.
Controls listen for pointer and wheel events on the canvas. If your own click handler also uses the canvas, decide which one should own the gesture.

lessons.task: Add OrbitControls with damping and update them every frame.
hints: Pass the camera and `renderer.domElement` to `new OrbitControls(...)`.
Set `controls.enableDamping = true` and call `controls.update()` in the loop.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: When would orbit controls compete with a click-to-select interaction, and how would you resolve it?

lessons.title: 7. Picking with a raycaster
lessons.summary: Convert pointer coordinates to normalized device coordinates, then shoot a ray through the camera.

activities.title: From click to hit
activities.instruction: `Raycaster.setFromCamera` expects x and y in the -1..1 range. Use the canvas bounding rect, not the whole window, so the math still works when the canvas is embedded.

activities.title: What range does the raycaster expect?
activities.question: What coordinate range does `raycaster.setFromCamera(pointer, camera)` expect?
choices: 0 to canvas width and 0 to canvas height
-1 to 1 on both axes
0 to 1 on both axes
activities.explanation: It uses normalized device coordinates: x runs -1 (left) to 1 (right), and y runs -1 (bottom) to 1 (top).

activities.title: Pick the cube
activities.instruction: Create a raycaster, set it from the pointer and camera, and intersect the scene's meshes.

teaching.text: Picking is a CPU-side ray cast against object bounds, not a GPU color read. Keep the candidate list small and pass `recursive` only when child objects should be tested too.
A click that both selects an object and orbits the camera can feel ambiguous. Use pointerup, drag thresholds, or separate UI affordances.

lessons.task: Shoot a ray from the pointer and intersect the scene's meshes.
hints: Create `new THREE.Raycaster()` and a `THREE.Vector2()` for the pointer.
Call `raycaster.setFromCamera(pointer, camera)` and then `raycaster.intersectObjects(scene.children, true)`.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why should a pick test use the canvas bounding rect instead of `window.innerWidth`?

lessons.title: 8. Loading a glTF model
lessons.summary: Load a model asynchronously, add its root to the scene, and configure its meshes for shadows.

activities.title: Load, inspect, add
activities.instruction: `gltf.scene` is a group containing the imported model. `traverse` visits every child so you can set shadows or swap materials without knowing the model's internal structure.

activities.title: What is gltf.scene?
activities.question: What is `gltf.scene` in a `GLTFLoader` callback?
choices: A single mesh
The root Object3D of the loaded model
The raw binary file
activities.answer: The root Object3D of the loaded model
activities.explanation: The model may contain many meshes, cameras, and nested groups. `gltf.scene` is the root you add to your own scene.

activities.title: Load and add the model
activities.instruction: Use `GLTFLoader` to load `/models/robot.glb`, configure its meshes, and add `gltf.scene` to the scene.

teaching.text: Models load over the network, so the rest of the scene must render while they are missing. Add a loading indicator, handle failures, and do not block the animation loop waiting for a file.
Compressed models need `DRACOLoader` or `MeshoptDecoder` configured before loading. Check the file size and texture budget on a mid-range phone, not only on your desktop.

lessons.task: Load `/models/robot.glb`, configure its meshes, and add it to the scene.
hints: Create `const loader = new GLTFLoader()` and call `loader.load(...)`.
Inside the success callback, add `gltf.scene` to the scene.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: What should the user see while a large model is still downloading?

tracks.name: Production Scenes
tracks.description: Use textures correctly, cut draw calls, add post-processing, and release GPU memory.

lessons.title: 9. Textures and color space
lessons.summary: Color textures need the sRGB color space and sensible wrapping, filtering, and anisotropy.

activities.title: Load, color, tile
activities.instruction: Mark photographic or painted color maps as sRGB. Data maps such as normal, roughness, and metalness are linear and must not be marked as sRGB. Set wrapping before tiling with `repeat`.

activities.title: Washed-out color
activities.question: A color texture looks washed out compared with the source image. What is the likely cause?
choices: The texture is not marked as `SRGBColorSpace`
The camera has no shadows
The mesh is using too many vertices
activities.answer: The texture is not marked as `SRGBColorSpace`
activities.explanation: Color textures are authored in sRGB. Without that tag, three.js treats the values as linear and the output looks too bright or washed out.

activities.title: Load and tile a texture
activities.instruction: Load `/textures/grid.png`, mark it as sRGB, and tile it 4 by 4.

teaching.text: Color management is the difference between a render that matches the artist's file and one that looks muddy. Set the texture's color space at load time, not after the material first renders.
High anisotropy improves tilted-surface detail but costs memory bandwidth. `getMaxAnisotropy()` reports the GPU limit; clamp it to a value your budget allows.

lessons.task: Load the grid texture, mark it as sRGB color data, and tile it 4 by 4.
lessons.starterCode:
import * as THREE from 'three';

// Load /textures/grid.png, mark it as color, and tile it 4 by 4
hints: Start with `new THREE.TextureLoader().load('/textures/grid.png')`.
Set `texture.colorSpace`, both wrap modes, then `texture.repeat.set(4, 4)`.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Which texture maps should stay linear instead of sRGB, and why?

lessons.title: 10. Instancing and draw calls
lessons.summary: Draw hundreds of copies of one geometry in a single call instead of creating hundreds of meshes.

activities.title: One mesh, many transforms
activities.instruction: `InstancedMesh` stores one geometry and one material plus a per-instance transform matrix. Update the matrices once, then mark the instance matrix as needing an upload.

activities.title: Fewer draw calls
activities.question: You need 1,000 identical trees. Which approach produces fewer draw calls?
choices: 1,000 separate Mesh objects
One InstancedMesh with 1,000 instances
One Group containing 1,000 meshes
activities.explanation: A group does not merge draws. Instancing sends one geometry and one material with many transforms, so the GPU can draw the copies in one call.

activities.title: Build an instanced field
activities.instruction: Create an `InstancedMesh` of 500 cubes, set each instance matrix, and mark the matrix for upload.

teaching.text: Draw calls are often the bottleneck before triangle count is. Instancing helps when objects share geometry and material; it hurts when each copy needs different geometry, unique materials, or per-instance CPU logic every frame.
Moving one instance means updating its matrix and setting `instanceMatrix.needsUpdate` again. Recomputing all instances every frame gives back much of the CPU saving.

lessons.task: Create an InstancedMesh of 500 cubes and set every instance matrix.
hints: Pass geometry, material, and the count to `new THREE.InstancedMesh(...)`.
Use a dummy `Object3D`, call `updateMatrix()`, then `setMatrixAt(i, dummy.matrix)`.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: When is instancing a bad optimization compared with a handful of ordinary meshes?

lessons.title: 11. Post-processing
lessons.summary: Render through a composer when the final image needs bloom, depth of field, or color grading.

activities.title: Render through passes
activities.instruction: `EffectComposer` replaces a direct `renderer.render` call. Add a `RenderPass`, then effect passes, then `OutputPass` last so tone mapping and output color space are applied to the final image.

activities.title: Why OutputPass last?
activities.question: Why should `OutputPass` be the final pass in the composer?
choices: It adds the most color
It applies tone mapping and the renderer's output color space to the final image
It makes the scene load faster
activities.answer: It applies tone mapping and the renderer's output color space to the final image
activities.explanation: Earlier passes work in linear space. `OutputPass` performs the conversion the display expects, so it needs to come after the effects.

activities.title: Add a bloom pass
activities.instruction: Create an `EffectComposer`, add a `RenderPass`, then add an `UnrealBloomPass`.

teaching.text: Post-processing is a full-screen cost. Bloom renders bright areas into smaller buffers and blurs them; depth of field samples the scene repeatedly. Add one effect at a time and measure on the weakest device you support.
If the whole scene is soft or dim, fix lighting and materials before adding a corrective post effect. Effects amplify a good render; they rarely rescue a flat one.

lessons.task: Build a composer with a RenderPass and an UnrealBloomPass.
lessons.starterCode:
import * as THREE from 'three';

// Create the composer, add a RenderPass, then a UnrealBloomPass
hints: The composer takes the renderer: `new EffectComposer(renderer)`.
Add `new RenderPass(scene, camera)` before the bloom pass.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: How would you decide whether a blurry, low-contrast image needs post-processing or better lighting?

lessons.title: 12. Disposal and shipping
lessons.summary: Stop the loop and release geometries, materials, textures, and the renderer when a scene is torn down.

activities.title: Release what the GPU owns
activities.instruction: Removing a mesh from the scene does not free its GPU buffers. Dispose geometries, materials, and textures; stop the animation loop; remove listeners; and dispose the renderer when the view unmounts.

activities.title: Does removal free memory?
activities.question: You call `scene.remove(cube)`. Are the cube's geometry and material GPU buffers freed?
choices: Yes, removing always frees them
No, you must dispose the geometry and material
Only if the cube cast a shadow
activities.answer: No, you must dispose the geometry and material
activities.explanation: The scene graph is a reference graph. GPU resources live until `dispose()` is called, so a long-lived page that swaps scenes leaks without cleanup.

activities.title: Write a cleanup function
activities.instruction: Stop the animation loop, remove the resize listener, dispose the scene's geometries and materials, and dispose the renderer.

teaching.text: A three.js view is an application with a lifecycle. In a single-page app, mounting and unmounting routes can create and destroy many renderers. Treat cleanup as part of the feature, not an afterthought.
Dispose only resources your code owns. A shared geometry or texture used by another live view should stay alive until every user is done with it.

lessons.task: Write a cleanup function that stops rendering and releases GPU resources.
hints: Call `renderer.setAnimationLoop(null)` to stop frames.
Traverse the scene, then call `dispose()` on geometry, material, and the renderer.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: What leaks when a single-page app mounts a new three.js scene on every route change without cleanup?
